[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional parties and reference number]

LEGAL NOTICE — CEASE AND DESIST
Ref. LN/2026/0417 | Issued 08 August 2026 | Reply by 23 August 2026

On behalf of our client Shri R. M. Deshpande, we address this notice to the Cockroach Janta Party (Noticee No. 1) and to the Nodal Officer of the hosting intermediary (Noticee No. 2).

On 06 August 2026 the Noticee published a three-slide carousel described as a press briefing of its National Working Committee. Slide 3 asserts that the political environment is marked by the targeted misuse of state agencies, widespread horse-trading of elected representatives, and engineered party splits. While our client is not named in terms, the surrounding matter and the Noticee's contemporaneous posts render the imputation capable of being understood as referring to him.

Our client states that no proceeding, finding or order of any competent authority supports the imputations as they attach to him, and that the Noticee published without seeking his comment.

The Noticees are called upon to: (a) take down the impugned carousel within fifteen days of receipt; (b) publish an unconditional retraction in the same medium, pinned for seven days; and (c) preserve all drafts, internal communications and analytics relating to the publication.

Failing compliance, our client will initiate proceedings under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and move for an injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC. Costs of this notice are quantified at Rs. 55,000.

[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional court, parties and order]

INTERIM ORDER — CS(OS) 1182/2026
Court of the learned District Judge-3, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar | Heard 10 August 2026

Heard learned counsel for the applicant and counsel appearing on advance notice for both defendants. Perused the plaint, the application under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC, and the annexures.

Slides 1 and 2 of the impugned publication are, on a plain reading, an announcement of a listening tour and of a membership drive, and contain no reference, direct or oblique, to the applicant. So far as slide 3 is concerned, the imputations are couched in general terms; whether the innuendo pleaded is made out is a matter for trial. The balance of convenience does not favour suppression of political speech in its entirety at an ex parte stage.

Interim arrangement: (a) Defendant No. 2 shall within 72 hours restrict access to slide 3 for viewers within the territorial limits of this district; (b) Defendant No. 2 shall preserve access logs, upload metadata and takedown records; (c) Defendant No. 1 is restrained from republishing the imputation in identical terms until the next date.

Notice on the suit and on the application, returnable on 14 September 2026. Reply within three weeks with an advance copy to the other side. Nothing in this order shall be construed as an expression of opinion on the merits.

[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional grievance reference and correspondence]

INTERMEDIARY NOTICE — GRIEVANCE FORWARDED
MEITY/GRV/2026/22318 | Issued 09 August 2026 | Disposal by 24 August 2026

A grievance dated 07 August 2026 has been received alleging that a carousel publication of 06 August 2026 contains imputations defamatory of the complainant. The URL, the account handle, the timestamp and the specific slide complained of are reproduced at Annexure I.

The intermediary is required to acknowledge the grievance within twenty-four hours of receipt and to dispose of it within fifteen days under Rule 3(2)(a) of the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. Where removal is declined, reasons must be communicated to the complainant along with the right to appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee within thirty days.

The intermediary shall not remove content merely upon receipt of this communication where it is of the view that removal is not warranted; the decision, and the reasons for it, must be recorded.

Information sought: whether the content has been removed, restricted, labelled or retained without action, with date and time of each step; whether any prior grievance on the same account or content was received in the preceding six months; and the particulars of the Resident Grievance Officer who dealt with the matter. Records are to be preserved for 180 days.

Status: compliance pending — acknowledgement not received as on 12 August 2026.

[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional FIR number, police station and accused]

FIRST INFORMATION REPORT 0349/2026
Cyber Police Station, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar | Occurrence 05 August 2026 | Registered 06 August 2026

Statement of the informant, Shri D. Pawar, 44, venue security supervisor: I was deployed at Gate 2 of the venue on 05 August 2026 for a two-day session of a political organisation. At about 11:20 hours, two persons presented press accreditation passes numbered PRS-1147. The scanner recorded that a pass bearing the same number had already been scanned at 09:04 hours the same morning. On being asked to wait, both persons handed over the passes and walked towards the parking area. They did not return.

Property seized: two laminated accreditation passes bearing the serial PRS-1147, each carrying a photograph and a QR code; and one handwritten entry-register page for Gate 2 covering 09:00 to 12:00 hours.

Sections invoked: Section 336 (forgery) and Section 340 (using as genuine a forged document) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in the alternative.

Action taken: investigation taken up by the undersigned; CCTV footage of Gate 2 and the parking area for 09:00 to 12:30 hours requisitioned from the venue management; the organisation's media cell asked to furnish the master list of accreditations issued.

Status: under investigation. No arrest effected as on the date of this record.

[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional RTI reference and reply]

REPLY UNDER SECTION 7(1) OF THE RIGHT TO INFORMATION ACT, 2005
RTI/CP/2026/1147 | Application 14 July 2026 | Replied 30 July 2026

Point 1: Fourteen applications for permission to hold public gatherings were received for the period 01 July 2026 to 15 August 2026. Eleven were granted with conditions, two were refused, and one was withdrawn by the applicant organisation.

Point 2: The standard conditions imposed include restriction of the gathering to the sanctioned venue and timings, a cap on amplification equipment after 22:00 hours, deployment of the organiser's own volunteers in a stated ratio, and prior intimation of any change in route. The template is enclosed at Annexure A; individual permission letters may be inspected at this office on any working day between 11:00 and 16:00 hours.

Point 3: The two refusals were recorded on the ground of an overlapping permission already granted at the same venue for the same date, and on the ground of an inadequate parking and egress plan.

Point 4: Information concerning internal threat assessments, deployment strength and the identity of reporting officers is denied under Section 8(1)(g), disclosure being likely to endanger the safety of the personnel concerned.

Appellate remedy: a first appeal lies to the First Appellate Authority within thirty days of receipt of this reply. No fee is payable.

[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional deponent and affidavit]

COMPLIANCE AFFIDAVIT — AFF/2026/8891
Sworn before a Notary at Mumbai on 11 August 2026 | Filed in CS(OS) 1182/2026

I, Ms. K. Raman, aged 39, am the Resident Grievance and Nodal Officer of the second defendant and am authorised to swear this affidavit. The facts stated are derived from records maintained in the ordinary course of business.

The order dated 10 August 2026 was received through the designated channel at 16:42 hours on 10 August 2026. Access to slide 3 of the impugned publication was restricted for viewers originating within the territorial limits of the district at 09:15 hours on 11 August 2026, being within the seventy-two hours allowed. Slides 1 and 2 remain accessible, no direction having been made in respect of them.

A legal hold has been placed on the account, the publication identifier, the upload metadata, the edit history and the access logs. The held records will not be deleted, overwritten or subjected to routine retention purges until this Court directs otherwise.

The second defendant is an intermediary and does not initiate the transmission, select the receiver, or select or modify the information transmitted. Nothing herein is an admission of the truth or falsity of the impugned content, or a waiver of any defence including under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

Verification: the contents of paragraphs 1 to 4 are true to my knowledge derived from records; no part of it is false and nothing material has been concealed.

[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional petition, petitioners and case number]

PUBLIC INTEREST PETITION UNDER ARTICLE 226 — PIL 214/2026
High Court of Judicature at Bombay | Filed 03 August 2026 | Next hearing 22 September 2026

Petitioner No. 1 is a registered trust that has conducted media literacy programmes in eleven districts; Petitioner No. 2 has published peer-reviewed work on political information flows. The petition raises no private grievance and seeks no monetary relief.

Political organisations increasingly publish policy positions as image carousels rather than as text, with the consequence that the content is not indexed, not searchable, and not amenable to automated fact-checking. A carousel published on 06 August 2026 by a national pressure group illustrates the difficulty: the text exists only as pixels, and any subsequent edit leaves no visible trace. Where such content is actioned on a grievance, neither the reason nor the fact of the action is published.

Grounds: that Article 19(1)(a) includes the right of the listener to know the provenance of political communication addressed to the electorate; that the absence of any published labelling standard results in arbitrariness offending Article 14; and that takedowns effected without a reasoned, communicated order are inconsistent with the procedural discipline read into blocking powers.

Prayer: (a) direct MeitY to frame, after consultation, a standard for provenance metadata on political content; (b) direct the intermediary to publish aggregate, anonymised data on grievances relating to political content and their outcomes; (c) direct that every takedown of political content be accompanied by a reasoned order communicated to the originator.

Status: admitted; notice issued.

[SYNTHETIC SAMPLE — fictional judgment, bench and parties; not to be cited]

JUDGMENT — WP(C) 5540/2025
High Court of Judicature at Bombay | Reserved 19 May 2026 | Pronounced 27 June 2026

The question is whether a fact-checking body that applies a 'context added' label to a third-party post thereby publishes a defamatory imputation of its own.

The distinction that matters is between a label directed at the claim and a label directed at the claimant. 'This photograph is from 2019' is of the first kind. 'This account repeatedly misleads' is of the second. A label of the first kind, which states a verifiable fact and links to the material relied on, is protected comment on a matter of public interest; the ordinary reasonable reader does not understand it as an attack on character. A label of the second kind makes an assertion about a person, and the maker must be prepared to justify it in the ordinary way — safe harbour is of no assistance, because in adding such a label the body ceases to be a conduit and becomes an author.

On the material before us the impugned label was of the first kind. It identified the date and origin of a photograph and linked to two archival sources. No imputation concerning the second respondent's character arises.

Held: labelling bodies should record, and be able to produce, the material relied on and any right of reply offered before a label is applied. The writ petition is allowed; the impugned proceedings, so far as the petitioner is concerned, stand quashed. No order as to costs.
